Section(s): 2.8. Volume change; 2.9. Heat of reaction; 2.10. CO_{2} evolution

Text and equations in reading order:
    The fed-batch process operation causes a volume change in the fermentor. This is calculated by:
(14) \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=F+F_{\mathrm{a/b}}-F_{\mathrm{loss}}    [code: ODE, computes V, code proposes balance]
    In order to consider the effect of acid/base addition on the total volume change of the culture broth, we have included the second term, $ F_{a/b} $. We have also included the $ F_{loss} $ term to account for evaporative loss during fermentation. The loss in volume due to evaporation is in fact more significant in industrial fermentations than the base addition term. Normally the air entering the fermentor is fairly dry and it is at about 90–100% relative humidity after bubbling through the broth. Typically, 10–20% of the total broth can be lost due to evaporation during 1 week of fermentation...
(15) F_{\mathrm{l o s s}}=V\lambda(\mathrm{e}^{5((T-T_{0})/T_{\mathrm{v}}-T_{0})}-1)    [code: algebraic, computes F_{loss}, code proposes constitutive]
    where $ T_0 $ and $ T_v $ are the freezing and boiling temperatures of the culture medium that were assumed to have the same properties as water, respectively. We have assumed that the evaporation rate will tend to infinity at the boiling point, and for engineering purposes the exponent 5 is large enough to represent this. $ \lambda $ is arranged to give an evaporation rate of $ 2.5 \times 10^{-4} $ l/h at the operation temperature (25 °C). This expression suggests including an evaporative loss term in volume due to temperature rather than proposing a mechanism. Since we do not base our $ F_{l...
(16) \frac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\mathrm{rxn}}}{\mathrm{d}t}=r_{q_{1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}X}{\mathrm{d}t}\ V+r_{q_{2}}\ X V    [code: ODE, computes Q_{rxn}, code proposes balance]
    Neglecting all other sources of heat generation except that caused by microbial reactions, the volumetric heat production rate is given as:
    ...small there is still significant heat generation from metabolic maintenance activities. Therefore, we have included the second term in Eq. (16) to account for the heat production during maintenance. Because the heat generation and $ CO_2 $ evolution show similar profiles, their production rate due to growth (dX/dt) and biomass (X) should have the same ratio as a first approximation. Based on this observation, $ r_{q_2} $ is calculated and tabulated in Table 2. The energy balance is written based on a coiled type heat exchanger which is suitable for a laboratory scale fermentor (Nielsen, 1997):
(17) \begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}=&\frac{F}{s_{\mathrm{f}}}(T_{\mathrm{f}}-T)+\frac{1}{V\rho c_{\mathrm{p}}}\\&\times\left[Q_{\mathrm{rxn}}-\frac{a F_{\mathrm{c}}^{b+1}}{F_{\mathrm{c}}+(a F_{\mathrm{c}}^{b}/2\rho_{\mathrm{c}}c_{\mathrm{pc}})}\right]\end{aligned}    [code: ODE, computes T, code proposes balance]
    A lab-scale fermentor was assumed in deciding to use a cooling coil, building the model, and developing the related equations. For industrial scale fermentors, the heat transfer mechanism should be modified to a jacketed fermentor with baffles and appropriate equations must be substituted.
    The introduction of variables which are easy to measure yet important in terms of their information content has been very helpful in predicting other important process variables. One such variable is $ CO_{2} $ from which biomass may be predicted with high accuracy. In this work, $ CO_{2} $ evolution is assumed to be due to growth, penicillin biosynthesis and maintenance requirements as suggested by Montague, Morris, Wright, Aynsley and Ward (1986). The $ CO_{2} $ evolution is:
(18) \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{CO}_{2}}{\mathrm{~d}t}=\alpha_{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}X}{\mathrm{d}t}+\alpha_{2}X+\alpha_{3}    [code: ODE, computes CO_{2}, code proposes balance]
    Here, the values of $ \alpha_1 $, $ \alpha_2 $ and $ \alpha_3 $ are chosen to give $ \text{CO}_2 $ profiles similar to the predictions of Montague et al. (1986). $ \text{CO}_2 $ evolution is nearly the same as oxygen demand for penicillin production using glucose as a substrate and $ \text{CO}_2 $ evolution trend levels off after the fed-batch switch as expected.

Symbols:
  V: Culture volume [l] (computed)
  F: feed flow rate of substrate [l/h] (variable)
  F_{a/b}: Term accounting for acid/base addition to the culture broth volume. [volume time^-1] (variable)
  F_{loss}: Evaporative loss from fermentation. [l h^-1] (computed)
  \lambda: Constant in the evaporative-loss law. [per h] (parameter)
  T: Temperature [K] (computed)
  T_{0}: Freezing temperature of the culture medium. (parameter)
  T_{v}: Boiling temperature of the culture medium. (parameter)
  Q_{rxn}: Heat generation. [cal] (computed)
  r_{q_1}: Yield coefficient for the biomass-growth contribution to heat generation. (parameter)
  X: Biomass concentration (computed)
  r_{q_2}: Coefficient multiplying biomass concentration and volume in the heat-generation law. (parameter)
  s_{f}: feed substrate concentration [g/l] (variable)
  T_{f}: Feed temperature of substrate. [K] (variable)
  \rho: Density component of the medium's density–heat-capacity term. (parameter)
  c_{p}: Specific heat capacity of the medium in the thermal balance. (parameter)
  a: Heat transfer coefficient of cooling/heating liquid [cal/h °C] (parameter)
  F_{c}: Cooling water flow rate [l/h] (variable)
  b: Constant exponent in the cooling-water heat-transfer expression [-] (parameter)
  \rho_{c}: Density × heat capacity of cooling liquid [per °C] (parameter)
  c_{pc}: Specific heat capacity of the cooling liquid (parameter)
  CO_{2}: Carbon dioxide concentration [mmol/l] (computed)
  \alpha_{1}: Constant relating CO₂ to growth [mmol CO₂/g biomass] (parameter)
  \alpha_{2}: Constant relating CO₂ to maintenance energy [mmol CO₂/g biomass h] (parameter)
  \alpha_{3}: Constant relating CO₂ to penicillin production [mmol CO₂/l h] (parameter)

laws.description: Culture-volume balance accounting for substrate feed, acid/base addition, and evaporative loss.
laws.quote: The fed-batch process operation causes a volume change in the fermentor. This is calculated by:
laws.law_type_reason: It gives the accumulation of culture volume as volume inputs minus evaporative loss.

laws.description: Temperature-dependent expression for the evaporative-loss rate from the culture volume.
laws.quote: We have also included the $ F_{loss} $ term to account for evaporative loss during fermentation.
laws.law_type_reason: It specifies an empirical relation for the evaporation rate rather than a conservation balance.

assumptions.text: The freezing and boiling temperatures are taken to be those of water.
assumptions.quote: where $ T_0 $ and $ T_v $ are the freezing and boiling temperatures of the culture medium that were assumed to have the same properties as water, respectively.

assumptions.text: The evaporation rate is assumed to tend to infinity at the boiling point, with exponent 5 used to approximate this behavior.
assumptions.quote: We have assumed that the evaporation rate will tend to infinity at the boiling point, and for engineering purposes the exponent 5 is large enough to represent this.

laws.issue: As printed, the exponent is finite at T = T_v and subtracts the temperature T_0 from a dimensionless ratio, inconsistent with the stated divergence at boiling and dimensionally inconsistent.

laws.description: Heat-generation rate from biomass growth and biomass-associated maintenance activity.
laws.quote: Neglecting all other sources of heat generation except that caused by microbial reactions, the volumetric heat production rate is given as:
laws.law_type_reason: It prescribes an empirical heat-generation rate from growth and biomass rather than closing an energy inventory balance.

assumptions.text: All heat-generation sources other than microbial reactions are neglected.
assumptions.quote: Neglecting all other sources of heat generation except that caused by microbial reactions

assumptions.text: Growth-related heat and biomass-associated heat are taken to have the same ratio as a first approximation.
assumptions.quote: Because the heat generation and $ CO_2 $ evolution show similar profiles, their production rate due to growth (dX/dt) and biomass (X) should have the same ratio as a first approximation.

laws.issue: The text calls this a volumetric heat-production rate, but both right-hand-side terms are multiplied by V and Q_{rxn} is defined in calories, so the equation represents a total heat-generation rate.

laws.description: Temperature balance for a fed-batch fermentor with feed-temperature exchange, reaction heat, and cooling-coil heat removal.
laws.quote: The energy balance is written based on a coiled type heat exchanger which is suitable for a laboratory scale fermentor (Nielsen, 1997):
laws.law_type_reason: It is an energy balance that computes the temperature change from feed and heat-generation and removal terms.

assumptions.text: A lab-scale fermentor with a cooling coil is assumed for the model and its related equations.
assumptions.quote: A lab-scale fermentor was assumed in deciding to use a cooling coil, building the model, and developing the related equations.

laws.issue: The feed term uses F/s_f, but s_f is defined as substrate concentration, making the term dimensionally inconsistent with a temperature-rate balance; a volume term such as V appears to be missing or misprinted.

laws.description: Carbon-dioxide evolution rate represented as contributions from biomass growth, maintenance, and penicillin production.
laws.law_type_reason: It is an empirical carbon-dioxide production-rate expression, not a conservation balance with inlets and outlets.

assumptions.text: Carbon-dioxide evolution is attributed to growth, penicillin biosynthesis, and maintenance.
assumptions.quote: In this work, $ CO_{2} $ evolution is assumed to be due to growth, penicillin biosynthesis and maintenance requirements as suggested by Montague, Morris, Wright, Aynsley and Ward (1986).
